1) Answer

A reasonable proof that Olaf Scholz values human rights rests on his public commitments, the strategic documents issued by his government, and concrete policies implemented since he became Chancellor in December 2021:

- Explicit public commitment: In his address to the UN General Assembly on 20 September 2022, Scholz underscored Germany’s “obligation to respect and to defend human rights at all times and in all places,” framing dignity, freedom and protection from harm as universal. This is a primary-source statement from the Chancellor. ([new-york-un.diplo.de](https://new-york-un.diplo.de/un-en/2553516-2553516?utm_source=openai))

- Government strategy that centers human rights: The National Security Strategy adopted on 21 June 2023 states that Germany will stand up for “the fundamental values … the Charter of the United Nations, human rights and international law.” It embeds “integrated security” with individual security and rights at its core and is signed by Scholz. ([auswaertiges-amt.de](https://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/blueprint/servlet/resource/blob/2604006/857b2e75fade2a89cc5232a59fca997b/nationale-sicherheitsstrategie-data.pdf))

- Institutionalized human-rights policy: The Federal Government’s Sixteenth Report on Human Rights Policy (covering 1 Oct 2022–30 Sep 2024, published 18 Dec 2024) opens by affirming that “upholding and advancing human rights is a key pillar” of government work domestically and abroad—codifying a cross‑government mandate during Scholz’s term. ([publikationen-bundesregierung.de](https://www.publikationen-bundesregierung.de/pp-en/search-for-publications/human-rights-policy-report-16-2339016?utm_source=openai))

- Protection of displaced people at scale: Under Scholz, Germany remained Europe’s largest host country for refugees and one of UNHCR’s largest bilateral donors. UNHCR reports about 2.7 million registered refugees in Germany by end‑2024 (3.1 million people under UNHCR’s mandate in 2024), reflecting sustained protection commitments aligned with human-rights obligations. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/countries/germany?utm_source=openai))

- Domestic rights reform for gender identity: The Self‑Determination Act (SBGG) passed the Bundestag on 12 April 2024 and entered into force on 1 November 2024, removing invasive assessments and a court process for legal gender and name change. This directly advances the dignity and equality of trans, intersex and nonbinary people—clear, rights‑enhancing legislation under Scholz’s government. ([bundestag.de](https://www.bundestag.de/dokumente/textarchiv/2024/kw15-de-geschlechtseintrag-997406?utm_source=openai))

- Human‑rights‑oriented foreign policy guidance: In March 2023 the Federal Foreign Office issued “Shaping Feminist Foreign Policy” guidelines that prioritize “rights, representation and resources” for marginalized groups across all external action; these guidelines have since been operationalized in humanitarian assistance. These are ministerial policies within Scholz’s cabinet and reflect a value‑based external posture. ([publikationen-bundesregierung.de](https://www.publikationen-bundesregierung.de/pp-en/search-for-publications/feminist-foreign-policy-2193650?utm_source=openai))

- Value‑driven China policy: The Federal Government’s China Strategy (21 July 2023) explicitly identifies concern over China’s attempts to relativize human rights, situating fundamental rights as a fixed benchmark for engagement and “de‑risking.” This anchors human‑rights standards in one of Germany’s most consequential bilateral relationships. ([auswaertiges-amt.de](https://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/blueprint/servlet/resource/blob/2608578/810fdade376b1467f20bdb697b2acd58/china-strategie-data.pdf))

- Development policy anchored in rights: The BMZ Human Rights Strategy (30 April 2024) states that human rights are the universal basis for a life in freedom, dignity and equality and sets out how development cooperation should realize those rights—another cabinet‑level instrument during Scholz’s term. ([publikationen-bundesregierung.de](https://www.publikationen-bundesregierung.de/pp-en/search-for-publications/human-rights-strategy-2280590?utm_source=openai))

Taken together—Scholz’s own on‑record UN commitment; cabinet‑adopted strategies that name human rights as foundational; major pro‑rights domestic legislation; and sustained protection for refugees—the evidence supports the claim that Olaf Scholz values human rights. As with any head of government, implementation can involve trade‑offs or contested choices in specific crises; nonetheless, the documents and policies above show a consistent, formalized prioritization of human rights in words, frameworks, and actions. ([new-york-un.diplo.de](https://new-york-un.diplo.de/un-en/2553516-2553516?utm_source=openai))
